content:
Oxfam has set up a monitoring station on the rooftop of a building in Yau Ma Tei to collect wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) data, believing it better reflects the actual heat conditions in the district.

Under the Labour Department's new work heat stress warning mechanism, if the Hong Kong Observatory has already issued the Extreme Hot Weather Special Advisory, a Red warning can be issued as long as the Hong Kong Heat Index reaches 32 at King's Park monitoring station or two of the other nine stations; when it reaches 34, a Black warning can likewise be issued with just a "two out of nine" condition. In addition, when temperatures across many parts of Hong Kong reach 35 degrees or above, the index thresholds for triggering the warnings mentioned above are further lowered, and the existing heat stress warning will be automatically raised by one level.

Dr Leung Ming-fung, Oxfam Hong Kong Programme Director, believes the current practice of issuing the "Work Heat Stress Warning" is inaccurate, due to the geographic locations of the monitoring stations and the different times when various districts experience peak heat. He recommended setting up WBGT monitors in all 18 districts of Hong Kong and arranging rest breaks for nearby workers according to the situation in each district.

The ten monitoring stations from which the Hong Kong Observatory collects heat stress data are located at King's Park, Beas River, Hong Kong Observatory, Sha Tin, Kau Sai Chau, Kowloon Bay, Happy Valley, Wong Chuk Hang, Chek Lap Kok and Wetland Park. Oxfam has set up its own six monitoring stations in Kwai Chung, Tsuen Wan, Yau Ma Tei, Taikoo, Admiralty and Tung Chung to collect data.

Dr Leung Ming-fung, Oxfam Hong Kong Programme Director, recommended setting up WBGT monitors in all 18 districts of Hong Kong and arranging rest breaks for nearby workers according to the situation in each district.

Monitoring stations in same district differ by up to 4.4 degrees in peak temperature

Comparing data from the Observatory and Oxfam, on 9 August the highest 60-minute average WBGT at King's Park was 32 degrees, while Oxfam's station in Yau Ma Tei recorded 36.6 degrees, a difference of 4.4 degrees. As for the period from 3 to 8 August, the gap in highest 60-minute average WBGT between King's Park and Yau Ma Tei was around 2 to 3 degrees.

Oxfam provided data from its six self-set up monitoring stations to the Collective, and used the internationally accepted "wet bulb globe temperature" to simulate the "Work Heat Stress Warning" from 3 to 9 August. The results found that within those six days, all districts reached the "Black Work Heat Stress Warning" level on each day, and on one additional day some districts reached the "Red Work Heat Stress Warning" level.

Leung explained that geographic and environmental factors cause the temperature gap between two stations in the same district to be very large. He described the King's Park monitoring station's location as a "fairyland" — a breezy spot at high elevation with no buildings nearby. In contrast, the Yau Ma Tei station sits on the rooftop of a tong lau in the middle of the city, surrounded by tall buildings, more closely reflecting the real-life conditions experienced in buildings or on the streets.

Leung added that most of the Observatory's monitoring stations are set up in open, hilly or rural areas, yet WBGT readings can be affected by where the sensor is placed. For example, sensors in densely built-up, poorly ventilated locations will produce very different readings. The six stations Oxfam has set up have their sensors placed near tall buildings and refuse collection points to reflect the actual conditions faced by outdoor workers at their workplaces.

Peak heat times vary greatly between monitoring stations

Between 15 May 2023 and 15 August 2026, the Labour Department issued a total of 209 "Yellow Work Heat Stress Warnings", but never issued any "Red" or "Black" Work Heat Stress Warnings. Leung explained that the "yellow, red and black" warnings are so hard to trigger because the peak temperature timing differs from station to station, making it difficult to meet the "four out of nine" condition in the past.

Using the agency's monitoring station data for 9 August as an example, Leung noted that Kwai Chung's peak heat period was 1pm to 2pm; Tsuen Wan's was 3pm to 4pm; Admiralty's was 12pm to 1pm; Yau Ma Tei's was 3pm to 4pm; Taikoo's was 9am to 10am; and Tung Chung's was 11am to noon.

Oxfam's monitoring station in Yau Ma Tei is surrounded by tall buildings.

3 to 9 August: at least "six days black" and "one day red"

Oxfam analysed the heat stress index from its six self-set up monitoring stations and used "wet bulb globe temperature" to simulate the "Work Heat Stress Warning" from 3 to 9 August, with the following results: on 9 August and 8 August, six districts reached "Black"; on 7 August, five districts reached "Black" and one reached "Red"; on 6 August, four districts reached "Black" and two reached "Red"; on 5 August, four districts reached "Black" and two reached "Red"; on 4 August, two districts reached "Black", three reached "Red" and one reached "Yellow"; on 3 August, two districts reached "Red" and one reached "Yellow".

A worker welding on a rooftop under the blazing sun, surrounded by tall buildings with poor ventilation.

Agency recommends WBGT monitors in all 18 districts

Leung suggested referencing overseas practices. For example, Singapore requires "wet bulb globe temperature instruments" to be set up at specific outdoor workplaces such as large construction sites, shipyards and processing yards; for other locations, data from 13 weather monitoring stations are used, with each station covering an average of about 57 square kilometres. Compared with Hong Kong, where each station covers an average of about 558 square kilometres, the difference is a factor of 10.

Street cleaning workers are most affected by weather changes.

Leung believes WBGT sensors should be set up in all 18 districts, or even at designated workplaces such as refuse collection points, and rest breaks should be arranged for workers according to the actual conditions of each district or workplace.
